H_hierarchical.evidence: The paper says the program is divided into upward and downward traversal, each with one-, two-, and three-floor cases, but this is organizational grouping rather than an explicit composite-state hierarchy.

G_guards_arith.evidence: Transitions are selected from current-floor counter/equality blocks plus requested-floor inputs; the results also distinguish same-floor, below-desired, and above-desired cases.

A_actions_nontrivial.evidence: Traversal rows include bit latching, working timers, motor outputs O:0/0 or O:0/1, and counter final-value updates; O0/O1 then drive clockwise or anti-clockwise motor motion.

F_fault_recovery.evidence: No emergency stop, fault state, rollback, or recovery transition is specified; 'checking of errors' refers only to setup testing.

T1_cross_section_element.evidence: The traversal cases and PLC output addresses are in the software-model section/table, while O0/O1-to-motor-direction mapping and same/below/above desired-floor behavior appear later in interfacing/results prose.

T2_implicit_domain_term.evidence: PLC terms such as equality block, TT bit, and normally-closed timer bits are explained by the paper rather than requiring unstated domain decoding.

T3_implicit_action_from_prose.evidence: The physical actions 'O0 -> clockwise/upward' and 'O1 -> anti-clockwise/downward' are attributed through later narrative prose, not solely in the traversal case definitions.

T4_multivar_arith_guard.evidence: Movement decisions combine current counter/floor, requested input floor, and timer-interlock conditions; results summarize guards as same, below, or above the desired floor.

T5_composite_internal_behavior.evidence: The upward/downward grouping has no parent entry, during, or exit behavior beyond the traversal cases.

T6_global_cross_cutting_recovery.evidence: No from-any-state fault or recovery rule is declared.

C1_speculative_dfs.evidence: No deep composite state, init pseudo-state chain, or non-trivial composite initialization is present.

C2_expr_ir_smt.evidence: Multiple floor-request combinations require counter/input comparisons and mutual-exclusion reasoning over timer bits, making a structured guard IR useful.

C3_forced_and_aspect.evidence: The same-floor no-run rule applies across floor states, and the normally-closed timer-bit rule prevents simultaneous timers across traversal cases.

C4_abstract_action.evidence: Outputs are concrete PLC/motor actions rather than effector-agnostic notifications, logs, or status publications.

key_nl_quotes: The program is divided into two parts, upward traversal of the elevator and downward traversal of the elevator. Each part is divided into three cases, one floor traversal, two floor traversal and three floor traversal.
When the elevator was below the desired floor, the motor ran in clockwise direction... When it was above the desired floor, the motor ran in anti-clockwise direction.
one_line_pitch: A compact elevator EFSM that forces extraction of floor-request guards, timer interlocks, counter updates, and motor-direction actions from tables plus separated prose.
rationale: This is a meaningful guard/action stress case because the controller depends on current-floor counters, requested-floor inputs, timer mutual exclusion, bit latching, motor outputs, and counter updates. It is also a baseline trap because the actionable semantics are split between the ladder-logic table and later hardware/results prose. It remains a backup rather than a top candidate because hierarchy is only shallow program grouping and the paper contains no real fault-recovery model.
